doc.title: Dianne Reeves interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, October 13, 2001

title: Meeting Clark Terry and the Broadmoor jazz party
summary: Terry heard her at a Chicago educators convention and brought her to Dick Gibson's jazz party, where she sang with great veterans.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: You had a fortuitous meeting with Clark Terry somewhere early on, didn’t you?

Yes. I met Clark — our jazz band won a city wide competition which allowed us to go to Chicago and perform for what was then called the National Association of Jazz Educators. And of course Clark has been affiliated with them for a long time. And he heard me and we started talking, and I didn’t know who he was, I just knew he was this nice man. My uncle was, “That’s Clark Terry” you know. And it’s like okay. So when he would come to Denver, there was this jazz party that this man Dick Gibson would give, at the Broadmoor. And the first jazz party that I ever did was with Clark. And he surrounded me with all these great musicians. Once again I still didn’t know who they were. My uncle would have to go back and give me records and say, “See this is this person, this is this person, that’s who you were performing with.” And sometimes it would be George Duvivier on bass or Major Holley, which was pretty amazing, or a lot of times it would be Louieyuo Bellson on drums or Grady Tate, Roland Hanna, Jimmy © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Rowles. It was pretty amazing. Eddie “Lockjaw” Davis. And I would come there with all my music together. My uncle would help me get it together, my keys, and tell them how I wanted to do these little head arrangements, because I was really into that and Clark just stayed in touch. And from that point on we just continued to work together and we still do.
